notes.sec: Structural signals
notes.t: Norway, all zones. Four ratios, one per horizon — take-out rate (now), months of cover (0–6 months), implied biomass growth (the biological engine), cohort conversion (6–18 months). Each one is built by summing numerators and denominators across the selected zones, not by averaging the zone ratios. Every figure is only meaningful against the same calendar period a year earlier.

notes.sec: Take-out rate × implied growth × price — index base 100 = historical norm for that calendar month
notes.t: Each series is rebased so that 100 is the average value of that same calendar month across the whole history — every June against the mean of all Junes. That strips out seasonality and puts three different units on one scale. It does not compare N to N−1: that comparison is the vertical gap between the solid curve and the N−1 curve of the same colour. Take-out above 100 while implied growth sits at or below 100 is the borrowing-from-stock configuration. The price curve is national and does not respond to the zone filter — no price exists by production area. It is the Akvafakta monthly export value ÷ export volume, a descriptive context curve: testing showed price tracks contemporaneous harvest volume (r = −0.66 on year-on-year changes) with no usable lead from the supply ratios, so do not read it as a forecast. Gaps in the line are months with no report (May–November 2023 in particular).

notes.sec: Take-out rate × implied growth × price — index base 100 = historical norm for that calendar month
notes.t: Method. All four ratios come from the monthly Biomasseregisteret alone, with no additional source. Opening stock and opening biomass for month M are the closing figures reported for M−1. Dead biomass is approximated as dead count × average stock weight (mean of the opening and closing weight of the month) — the approximation is enough at this granularity. Known bias: the source gives release headcounts in two size bands (< 250 g and 250–500 g) but no weight, so newly stocked fish would otherwise register as biological growth. An assumed release weight is subtracted — 0.14 kg for < 250 g, 0.35 kg for 250–500 g (constants SMOLT_KG_ASSUMED / SMOLT_MID_KG_ASSUMED); fish released above 500 g are not in the file and still show up as growth; because stocking is strongly seasonal, the year-on-year comparison of the same calendar month largely neutralises whatever the true figure is. The lag in ratio 4 is not a round year: it is the harvest-count-weighted mean time at sea over the last 36 months for the selected zones, currently 14.1 months, rounded to 14. Ratio 4 now divides by global smolt released (< 250 g + 250–500 g). With the < 250 g column alone it read above 1 — not a data error but a quarter of the fish (the 250–500 g band) missing from the denominator, a share that has doubled since 2018. It is still not a clean survival rate: fish released above 500 g and transfers between zones are not in the denominator, so read it as a year-on-year change. Note also that ratio 1 divides

notes.sec: Stock rotation — how fast the fish in the sea are turned into harvest
notes.t: Biomass rotation = tonnes harvested over 12 months ÷ average standing biomass: how many times a year the biomass in the sea is turned into harvest. Fish rotation = fish harvested ÷ average number of fish in the sea. With biomass capped by the licences (MTB), a faster rotation — larger smolts, shorter time at sea, more cycles per licence — is the only way to harvest more. Month by month the ratio is seasonal, so each month is read against the same month a year earlier. MTB by year is not available: only the current licence register is collected (BarentsWatch, 2026-11-06); earlier years will build up from now on.

notes.t: Estimated biomass (kt, live) of fish above 6.75 kg live (6 kg gutted), by generation, last 36 months; dashed line = same month a year earlier. Each zone and generation is assumed to have a log-normal weight spread (coefficient of variation 0.3) around its average weight. Why this rather than the old “generations above 5 kg” rule: tested on 2018–2026, this estimate two months ahead follows the share of 6 kg+ fish in Norway's weekly harvest (Akvafakta) with a correlation of 0.76 (0.47 once the seasonal pattern is removed), against 0.41 (0.17) for the rule that counts a whole generation once its average passes 5 kg. The level stays uncertain; the trend is what counts. Projection (hatched, next 6 months) = the same month a year earlier × today's ratio to a year earlier, that ratio fading back to 1 over six months; from two months ahead the ratio is the one of the 5–6 kg stock below, the fish that will feed the reservoir (error −12% at 2 months, −9% at 3 months when replayed); whiskers = 80% of the errors this method made when replayed on 2019–2026 (±4/5/6/7/6/7 kt by month ahead). notes.t: Estimated number of fish in each size class (gutted weight), Norway, all zones, last 36 months: bars = fish at sea, dashed line = a year earlier, lower band = change vs a year earlier (green up, red down). notes.t: What the panel sells vs what Norway harvests. Akvafakta's size split comes from the SISALMONI index: 17 exporters (incl. Mowi, but neither SalMar nor Lerøy), about a third of spot sales of superior salmon to Europe. Solid line: 6 kg+ share of all fish harvested in Norway, estimated from the register (harvest weight of each zone and generation, spread 0.27, the one that best reproduces Akvafakta). On average the panel sells 3.5 pt more 6 kg+ than Norway (superior grade for Europe only). When the dashed line drops below the solid one, big fish are being sold outside the panel. Last register month, Sep 2026: panel 5.8%, Norway 7.2% (gap -1.4 pt, usually +3.5). Back-test since 2020 (past data only): the reservoir forecasts the Norway share 2 months ahead with 1.51 pt error (−25% vs calendar alone), against 3.84 pt for the panel share (−8%): the stock at sea is read well, what the panel sells is the hard part. Adding the Norway share or the panel–Norway gap to the panel forecast adds nothing beyond the sales-weight term already used (about 1% less error, worse in peak months): not used.

notes.sec: Mortality events — algae, jellyfish, oxygen, storms… all basins
notes.t: BarentsWatch only lists notifiable diseases: algal blooms, jellyfish, low oxygen or storms leave no trace there, though they can kill hundreds of thousands of fish in days (Chile lost about 40,000 t in 2016). Three ways to catch them: unusual deaths in the Norwegian register (about 3 weeks after the month), events entered with their losses, and a press watch in every basin (within days).

notes.sec: Norway — unusual monthly deaths in the register
notes.t: Zone-months where the share of the fish present that died is at least twice the zone's usual level for that month (median of the other years) and 1.5 points above it, with at least 200,000 dead fish. Cause: an event recorded or found in the press for the same month; otherwise BarentsWatch is checked — new ILA/PD sites or a surge in lice treatments point to disease or handling; nothing there = unexplained (algae, jellyfish, oxygen, cold, handling…). Tonnes = dead fish × the zone's average live weight that month: an upper bound, since the small fish tend to die first.

notes.sec: Recorded events with losses
notes.t: Every basin, filled automatically at each news run: months with unusual deaths in each country's official data (Norway's biomass register by zone, MAST for Iceland, SEPA reports for Scotland — about six months late —, EPA mortality waste for Tasmania) and, where no data covers the month (Chile, Faroe Islands, Canada…), mortality stories taken up by the press, with the figures quoted in their titles. Events entered by hand from official statements come first and carry the cause. "Unusual" = at least twice the usual level of the zone.

notes.sec: 6 · By zone
notes.t: How to read it. Growth per fish = what the generation produced in the month (change in biomass + harvested kilos + dead fish at half weight) ÷ its average number of fish, so harvesting the biggest cages first does not lower it. Fish that appear or vanish without being declared (smolts put to sea, moves between registrations, count corrections) are taken in at 0.15 kg or out at the average weight, so they do not pass for growth or loss — in September 2026, 4.8 M G2025 fish vanished this way in zone 9 and 1.5 M in zone 12. TGC = (end weight^⅓ − start weight^⅓, in grams) × 1000 ÷ degree-days. Months at sea are worked out here, the same way for every generation, from the fish that arrive month by month (the register only gives the year the smolts went to sea), so they are close but not exact. Other definitions. Every figure compares the end of September 2026 with the end of September 2025. "Stocked" = fish at sea + fish already harvested + dead + lost since the generation went to sea (smolt numbers are not published by generation). Survival so far = 1 − (dead + lost) ÷ stocked. 5 kg+ / 6 kg+ = gutted weight classes estimated from each zone's average weight per generation. The month selector lets you replay any month of the last years; the tab updates by itself when the register publishes a new month (about five weeks after the month).

Two warning signs: volumes that do not match (the exporter declares much more or less than US customs records: re-exports or transit, as for UK exports, which include fish of other origins shipped through the UK), and a fillet declared below the value of the fish it is cut from (about 0.70 kg of fillet per kg of gutted fish: when fillet price × 0.70 is below the price of the whole gutted fish sent to the same market, the filleting would lose money — a price no independent buyer would get, typically a sale to a related company). notes.sec: Check of declared values — exporter's declaration against US customs
notes.t: How to read it. A price is shown only for months with at least 20 t shipped: a few parcels do not make a market price (Chile, for instance, sends almost no fresh fillets to Europe — its fresh fillets go to the US and Brazil). Export prices are the values each producer declares at export (Norway: Statistics Norway; other origins: their national statistics), so the US premium compares the same fish leaving the same country for two markets; for fresh product it includes the extra air freight to the US. Import prices are customs values recorded on arrival (US Census; Eurostat, EU arrivals from that origin). All are monthly averages mixing spot and contract sales, and they arrive with one to two months' delay. Wholesale quotes in the US (Miami, East Coast) are sold by private price services and are not included.

notes.sec: Monthly volumes by coast — fresh whole salmon into the US
notes.t: Canada sends almost all its fresh whole salmon to the United States by truck, and the US customs record the border post. Fish entering through Washington (Blaine) comes from British Columbia; fish entering through Maine (Calais, Houlton) comes from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. Posts on the Great Lakes and in New York (Detroit, Buffalo, Port Huron) cannot be tied to a coast and are kept apart. Share of value since 2018: BLAINE (WA) 55.7%, CALAIS (ME) 29.6%, DETROIT (MI) 9.1%, HOULTON (ME) 3.1%, BUFFALO-NIAGARA FALLS (NY) 1.1%, PORT HURON (MI) 0.6%. Road posts declare no weight: the tonnes of each coast are Canada's total tonnes (US Census, HTS 0302.14) shared out by the value through each post. This is the best monthly measure of each coast's harvest that is public, but it misses fish sold in Canada and air freight to Asia: in 2024 the Washington posts took about half of BC's harvest (27,108 t against 53,816 t live weight). Latest month: September 2026 (US Census, about five weeks after the month).

notes.sec: Harvest outlook — British Columbia, 2027 against 2026
notes.t: Harvest is projected from the cycle of each BC farm, since Canada publishes neither fish numbers nor weights. Every farm reports each month whether it is receiving smolts, growing or harvesting: that gives the date its fish went to sea. Since 2015, a BC farm started harvesting a median 15 months after its smolts went in (half between 12 and 17) and harvested for a median 5 months. Applied to the 23 farms with fish at sea at June 2026 (the last month DFO has published), this gives the farm-months of harvest expected each quarter; they are turned into tonnes with the volume per harvesting farm-month of the last 12 months (527 t, in US-import tonnes). Observed quarters are in plain type, projected ones in orange italics.

notes.sec: Harvest outlook — British Columbia, 2027 against 2026
notes.t: Reliability. The same projection was rerun from each quarter since 2023 with only the data known then: the next four quarters taken together were off by 13 % on average (+23, -2, -5, +8, +19, +30, +10, +11, +21, -11, -6 %). Single quarters are much less reliable (±34 % one quarter ahead) because harvests are bunched. The end of 2027 depends on smolts that are not yet at sea: they are assumed to be stocked as in the previous 12 months. What it does not see: the size of each farm, the weight of the fish, and a policy decision — open net-pen licences in BC expire on 30 June 2029, and companies have stopped restocking some farms. Mowi's guidance for Canada West is 23,000 t in 2027. Atlantic Canada publishes no farm-level data, so no projection is made for it: its monthly volumes are in the chart above (Maine ports).

notes.t: From DFO's monthly mortality reports: each BC Atlantic-salmon farm states whether it is receiving smolts ("smolt entry"), growing or harvesting that month. A farm receives smolts over one to three months. January–June: 25 farm-months of smolt entry in 2026 against 22 in 2025, and 46 farm-months of harvest against 28. notes.t: Monthly mean sea-surface temperature at a point at sea next to each farming area (Open-Meteo marine model, about 5 km grid; a model, not a farm sensor). BC water stays between about 8 and 13 °C all year, which is why its cycles are short; Newfoundland's south coast drops close to 0 °C in late winter, which limits growth and puts fish at risk of superchill.

notes.t: How the year is simulated. Each site is followed month by month from its fish and average weight: growth along Iceland's weight-by-months-at-sea curve (median of every site cycle since 2023: about 4 kg after 18 months, 5 kg after 22–24), each site keeping part of its advance or delay (scenarios: fades fast, central, kept), corrected by its sea temperature against its own normal; harvest = the share of the stock usually taken at that weight, higher once a site has started harvesting; mortality = Iceland's monthly average. Everything harvested in 2027 is already at sea. Tested from earlier months over the following 12: average error 6 % since spring 2025 (+5, -1, -4, +4, +17, +7, -5, -2, -3, -6, -4, -15 %); from 2024 the error was much larger (+40 to +95 %) because the site history then covered barely a year. Quarters are less reliable than the year. Projected quarters of 2026 are in italics.

notes.sec: Land-based farming — yearly production, sea against land (MAST)
notes.t: Atlantic salmon produced on land in 2025: 4,174 t (+17 % on 2024), 7.1 % of Iceland's salmon (sea 54,543 t). MAST publishes land farms only in its yearly figures (by region, not by company); the monthly dashboard covers sea cages only. Most of today's land-based salmon comes from the North; the large new projects (Landeldi and First Water at Þorlákshöfn, Laxey in the Westman Islands, Samherji's Eldisgarður at Reykjanes) are in the South and at Reykjanes and are still ramping up. Iceland also farms 5,141 t of Arctic char on land.

notes.sec: Cycle length — months at sea, site by site
notes.t: Months from the first month with fish in a site (after at least two empty months) to the month it is emptied, for every cycle completed since 2020-01. Iceland's cycles are long — cold water, slower growth, and most smolts stocked in spring and autumn. Runs shorter than 8 months (3 of them: fish moved, sites emptied early, the 2021-22 ISA outbreak in the east) are left out. 21 sites have fish now.
